questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
For the reduction of zinc oxide by carbon according to the reaction $\text{ZnO}(s) + \text{C}(s) \to \text{Zn}(s) + \text{CO}(g)$, the standard Gibbs free energy changes of oxidation per mole of $\text{O}_2$ consumed are given by:
$$2\text{Zn}(s) + \text{O}_2(g) \to 2\text{ZnO}(s), \quad \Delta G_1^\circ = -720 + 0.20\,T\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$
$$2\text{C}(s) + \text{O}_2(g) \to 2\text{CO}(g), \quad \Delta G_2^\circ = -220 - 0.20\,T\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$
where temperature $T$ is in Kelvin. Assuming unit activities for all solid species, determine the minimum temperature above which the carbothermic reduction of $\text{ZnO}$ becomes thermodynamically spontaneous.
questions.explanation: Step 1: Write the net reduction reaction by subtracting equation (1) from equation (2) and dividing by 2: $\text{ZnO}(s) + \text{C}(s) \to \text{Zn}(s) + \text{CO}(g)$. Step 2: The standard Gibbs free energy change of the net reduction reaction is: $\Delta G_{\text{rxn}}^\circ = \frac{1}{2}(\Delta G_2^\circ - \Delta G_1^\circ) = \frac{1}{2}\left[(-220 - 0.20\,T) - (-720 + 0.20\,T)\right] = \frac{1}{2}\left(500 - 0.40\,T\right) = 250 - 0.20\,T\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$. Step 3: Setting $\Delta G_{\text{rxn}}^\circ \le 0$ for spontaneity yields $250 - 0.20\,T \le 0$, which upon solving gives $T \ge \frac{250}{0.20} = 1250\text{ K}$. Distractor $1000\text{ K}$ arises from omitting the temperature coefficient of carbon, $1125\text{ K}$ results from using an incorrect divisor of $0.40$ without dividing by $2$, and $1500\text{ K}$ corresponds to an erroneous sign convention in the entropy change.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: In the MacArthur-Forrest hydrometallurgical extraction of gold from native ore, finely pulverized ore is leached with dilute sodium cyanide solution in the presence of atmospheric oxygen, followed by precipitation of gold using metallic zinc dust. According to the balanced stoichiometric equations, what are the minimum moles of dissolved $\text{O}_2$ gas and metallic $\text{Zn}$ dust required to successfully extract and precipitate exactly $2.0\text{ mol}$ of pure gold?
options: A) $0.50\text{ mol } \text{O}_2\text{ and } 1.00\text{ mol } \text{Zn}$
B) $1.00\text{ mol } \text{O}_2\text{ and } 1.00\text{ mol } \text{Zn}$
C) $0.50\text{ mol } \text{O}_2\text{ and } 2.00\text{ mol } \text{Zn}$
D) $0.25\text{ mol } \text{O}_2\text{ and } 0.50\text{ mol } \text{Zn}$
questions.explanation: Step 1: Write the balanced leaching equation for gold: $4\text{Au}(s) + 8\text{CN}^-(aq) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) + \text{O}_2(g) \to 4[\text{Au}(\text{CN})_2]^-(aq) + 4\text{OH}^-(aq)$. For $4\text{ mol}$ of $\text{Au}$, $1\text{ mol}$ of $\text{O}_2$ is consumed. Therefore, for $2.0\text{ mol}$ of $\text{Au}$, the required moles of $\text{O}_2$ are $n(\text{O}_2) = \frac{2.0}{4} = 0.50\text{ mol}$. Step 2: Write the displacement reaction with zinc: $2[\text{Au}(\text{CN})_2]^-(aq) + \text{Zn}(s) \to [\text{Zn}(\text{CN})_4]^{2-}(aq) + 2\text{Au}(s)$. For $2\text{ mol}$ of $\text{Au}$, exactly $1\text{ mol}$ of $\text{Zn}$ is oxidized. Hence, $n(\text{Zn}) = 1.00\text{ mol}$. Distractor B mistakenly assumes a 1:2 ratio for oxygen, distractor C assumes zinc reacts in a 1:1 molar ratio with gold, and distractor D halves the required quantities by miscounting gold stoichiometry.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: A $1000\text{ g}$ sample of bauxite ore containing $51.0\%\; \text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ and $6.0\%\; \text{SiO}_2$ by mass (with the balance being unreactive ferric oxide and titania) is digested with concentrated aqueous sodium hydroxide during Bayer's process. Alumina dissolves as sodium aluminate ($\text{Na}[\text{Al}(\text{OH})_4]$) and silica reacts as an acidic impurity to form soluble sodium silicate ($\text{Na}_2\text{SiO}_3$). Calculate the stoichiometric mass of pure $\text{NaOH}$ consumed in grams. (Molar masses: $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 = 102\text{ g mol}^{-1}$, $\text{SiO}_2 = 60\text{ g mol}^{-1}$, $\text{NaOH} = 40\text{ g mol}^{-1}$).
options: A) $400\text{ g}$
B) $480\text{ g}$
C) $560\text{ g}$
D) $240\text{ g}$
questions.explanation: Step 1: Calculate moles of reactive oxides in $1000\text{ g}$ of bauxite. Mass of $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 = 0.51 \times 1000 = 510\text{ g}$, so $n(\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3) = \frac{510}{102} = 5.0\text{ mol}$. Mass of $\text{SiO}_2 = 0.06 \times 1000 = 60\text{ g}$, so $n(\text{SiO}_2) = \frac{60}{60} = 1.0\text{ mol}$. Step 2: Write dissolution reactions: $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 + 2\text{NaOH} + 3\text{H}_2\text{O} \to 2\text{Na}[\text{Al}(\text{OH})_4]$, which requires $2\text{ mol } \text{NaOH}$ per mole of $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$, yielding $5.0 \times 2 = 10.0\text{ mol } \text{NaOH}$. For silica: $\text{SiO}_2 + 2\text{NaOH} \to \text{Na}_2\text{SiO}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$, which requires $2\text{ mol } \text{NaOH}$ per mole of $\text{SiO}_2$, yielding $1.0 \times 2 = 2.0\text{ mol } \text{NaOH}$. Step 3: Total moles of $\text{NaOH} = 10.0 + 2.0 = 12.0\text{ mol}$. Total mass of $\text{NaOH} = 12.0 \times 40 = 480\text{ g}$. Distractor A neglects the $\text{NaOH}$ consumed by silica gangue ($400\text{ g}$), distractor C doubles the silica consumption, and distractor D uses only $1\text{ mol } \text{NaOH}$ per mole of $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: In the Hall-Héroult electrolytic cell, molten alumina is reduced to aluminium metal at the cathode while the carbon anodes are progressively consumed by oxidation. If the evolved anode gases consist of an equimolar mixture of carbon monoxide ($\text{CO}$) and carbon dioxide ($\text{CO}_2$), calculate the theoretical mass of carbon anode consumed in kilograms to produce $54.0\text{ kg}$ of pure aluminium. (Atomic masses: $\text{Al} = 27\text{ g mol}^{-1}$, $\text{C} = 12\text{ g mol}^{-1}$, $\text{O} = 16\text{ g mol}^{-1}$).
options: A) $12.0\text{ kg}$
B) $18.0\text{ kg}$
C) $36.0\text{ kg}$
D) $24.0\text{ kg}$
questions.explanation: Step 1: Calculate moles of aluminium produced: $n(\text{Al}) = \frac{54000\text{ g}}{27\text{ g mol}^{-1}} = 2000\text{ mol}$. Step 2: From the formula $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$, the moles of oxygen atoms liberated from the reduction of $2000\text{ mol}$ of $\text{Al}$ are $n(\text{O}) = 2000 \times \frac{3}{2} = 3000\text{ mol}$. Step 3: Let the evolved gas contain $x\text{ mol}$ of $\text{CO}$ and $x\text{ mol}$ of $\text{CO}_2$ (equimolar). The total oxygen atoms in the gas mixture equal: $x + 2x = 3x = 3000\text{ mol}$, which gives $x = 1000\text{ mol}$. Step 4: The total moles of carbon consumed equal: $n(\text{C}) = n(\text{CO}) + n(\text{CO}_2) = x + x = 2000\text{ mol}$. Step 5: Hence, the mass of carbon consumed is $m(\text{C}) = 2000\text{ mol} \times 12\text{ g mol}^{-1} = 24000\text{ g} = 24.0\text{ kg}$. Distractor B corresponds to pure $\text{CO}_2$ evolution ($18.0\text{ kg}$), distractor C corresponds to pure $\text{CO}$ evolution ($36.0\text{ kg}$), and distractor A assumes half the carbon requirement.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: A batch of $97.5\text{ kg}$ of sphalerite ore containing $80.0\%\; \text{ZnS}$ by mass (molar mass of $\text{ZnS} = 97.5\text{ g mol}^{-1}$) is completely roasted in air according to $2\text{ZnS}(s) + 3\text{O}_2(g) \to 2\text{ZnO}(s) + 2\text{SO}_2(g)$. Assuming dry air contains $20.0\%\; \text{O}_2$ by volume and taking the standard molar volume of gas at STP as $22.4\text{ L mol}^{-1}$, determine the volume of dry $\text{SO}_2$ gas evolved at STP and the minimum volume of air required at STP.
options: A) $22.40\text{ m}^3\text{ of } \text{SO}_2\text{ and } 168.0\text{ m}^3\text{ of air}$
B) $17.92\text{ m}^3\text{ of } \text{SO}_2\text{ and } 134.4\text{ m}^3\text{ of air}$
C) $17.92\text{ m}^3\text{ of } \text{SO}_2\text{ and } 26.88\text{ m}^3\text{ of air}$
D) $35.84\text{ m}^3\text{ of } \text{SO}_2\text{ and } 268.8\text{ m}^3\text{ of air}$
questions.explanation: Step 1: Calculate mass of pure $\text{ZnS}$: $m(\text{ZnS}) = 0.80 \times 97.5\text{ kg} = 78.0\text{ kg} = 78000\text{ g}$. Moles of $\text{ZnS} = \frac{78000}{97.5} = 800\text{ mol}$. Step 2: From the reaction stoichiometry, $2\text{ mol } \text{ZnS} \equiv 2\text{ mol } \text{SO}_2$, so $n(\text{SO}_2) = 800\text{ mol}$. The volume of $\text{SO}_2$ at STP is $V(\text{SO}_2) = 800 \times 22.4\text{ L} = 17920\text{ L} = 17.92\text{ m}^3$. Step 3: Moles of $\text{O}_2$ consumed are $n(\text{O}_2) = 800 \times \frac{3}{2} = 1200\text{ mol}$. The volume of pure $\text{O}_2$ required at STP is $V(\text{O}_2) = 1200 \times 22.4\text{ L} = 26880\text{ L} = 26.88\text{ m}^3$. Step 4: Since air contains $20.0\%\; \text{O}_2$ by volume, the required volume of air is $V_{\text{air}} = \frac{26.88}{0.20} = 134.4\text{ m}^3$. Distractor A fails to account for the $80\%$ purity, distractor C confuses pure oxygen volume with air volume, and distractor D erroneously doubles the stoichiometry.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: During the smelting of haematite in a blast furnace, a charge contains $180\text{ kg}$ of acidic silica gangue ($\text{SiO}_2$, molar mass $60.0\text{ g mol}^{-1}$). To eliminate this gangue as fusible slag ($\text{CaSiO}_3$, molar mass $116.0\text{ g mol}^{-1}$), commercial limestone containing $80.0\%\; \text{CaCO}_3$ by mass (molar mass $100.0\text{ g mol}^{-1}$) is added. Assuming complete conversion, calculate the mass of commercial limestone required and the theoretical mass of slag produced.
options: A) $375\text{ kg commercial limestone and } 348\text{ kg slag}$
B) $300\text{ kg commercial limestone and } 348\text{ kg slag}$
C) $375\text{ kg commercial limestone and } 232\text{ kg slag}$
D) $450\text{ kg commercial limestone and } 412\text{ kg slag}$
questions.explanation: Step 1: Calculate moles of $\text{SiO}_2$ gangue: $n(\text{SiO}_2) = \frac{180000\text{ g}}{60.0\text{ g mol}^{-1}} = 3000\text{ mol}$. Step 2: Write slagging reactions: $\text{CaCO}_3 \to \text{CaO} + \text{CO}_2$ and $\text{CaO} + \text{SiO}_2 \to \text{CaSiO}_3$. One mole of $\text{CaCO}_3$ fluxes one mole of $\text{SiO}_2$. Hence, $3000\text{ mol}$ of pure $\text{CaCO}_3$ is required: $m_{\text{pure}}(\text{CaCO}_3) = 3000 \times 100.0\text{ g} = 300\text{ kg}$. Step 3: Accounting for $80.0\%$ purity, the mass of commercial limestone required is: $m_{\text{limestone}} = \frac{300\text{ kg}}{0.80} = 375\text{ kg}$. Step 4: The mass of slag formed is: $m(\text{CaSiO}_3) = 3000\text{ mol} \times 116.0\text{ g mol}^{-1} = 348000\text{ g} = 348\text{ kg}$. Distractor B neglects the limestone purity factor ($300\text{ kg}$), distractor C uses the formula mass of $\text{CaO}$ instead of $\text{CaSiO}_3$, and distractor D uses an inverted purity fraction.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: In the Bessemer converter stage of copper extraction, molten copper(I) sulfide ($\text{Cu}_2\text{S}$) undergoes self-reduction to blister copper via two successive reactions: partial roasting to copper(I) oxide ($\text{Cu}_2\text{O}$), followed by reaction between the oxide and unreacted sulfide: $2\text{Cu}_2\text{S} + 3\text{O}_2 \to 2\text{Cu}_2\text{O} + 2\text{SO}_2$ and $\text{Cu}_2\text{S} + 2\text{Cu}_2\text{O} \to 6\text{Cu} + \text{SO}_2$. What fraction of the initial $\text{Cu}_2\text{S}$ must be oxidized to $\text{Cu}_2\text{O}$ for complete self-reduction with zero residual reactant, and how many moles of $\text{O}_2$ are consumed per mole of blister copper ($\text{Cu}$) produced?
options: A) $\frac{1}{2}\text{ of } \text{Cu}_2\text{S}\text{ and } 1.00\text{ mol } \text{O}_2$
B) $\frac{1}{3}\text{ of } \text{Cu}_2\text{S}\text{ and } 0.25\text{ mol } \text{O}_2$
C) $\frac{2}{3}\text{ of } \text{Cu}_2\text{S}\text{ and } 0.50\text{ mol } \text{O}_2$
D) $\frac{3}{4}\text{ of } \text{Cu}_2\text{S}\text{ and } 0.75\text{ mol } \text{O}_2$
questions.explanation: Step 1: In the auto-reduction step, $1\text{ mol}$ of $\text{Cu}_2\text{S}$ requires $2\text{ mol}$ of $\text{Cu}_2\text{O}$. To produce $2\text{ mol}$ of $\text{Cu}_2\text{O}$, exactly $2\text{ mol}$ of $\text{Cu}_2\text{S}$ must be oxidized in step 1. Thus, out of every $3\text{ mol}$ of initial $\text{Cu}_2\text{S}$, $2\text{ mol}$ must be oxidized to $\text{Cu}_2\text{O}$ and $1\text{ mol}$ left as sulfide. Therefore, the required fraction is $\frac{2}{3}$. Step 2: Combining the two balanced equations: $(2\text{Cu}_2\text{S} + 3\text{O}_2) + (\text{Cu}_2\text{S} + 2\text{Cu}_2\text{O}) \to 2\text{Cu}_2\text{O} + 2\text{SO}_2 + 6\text{Cu} + \text{SO}_2$, which simplifies to: $3\text{Cu}_2\text{S} + 3\text{O}_2 \to 6\text{Cu} + 3\text{SO}_2$, or $\text{Cu}_2\text{S} + \text{O}_2 \to 2\text{Cu} + \text{SO}_2$. Step 3: The ratio of $\text{O}_2$ consumed to copper formed is $\frac{3\text{ mol } \text{O}_2}{6\text{ mol Cu}} = 0.50\text{ mol } \text{O}_2 / \text{mol Cu}$. Distractors A, B, and D stem from incorrectly balancing the consecutive stages.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
In an Ellingham diagram, the standard Gibbs free energy changes of formation per mole of $\text{O}_2$ for alumina and magnesia at temperatures above the boiling point of magnesium ($T > 1390\text{ K}$) are expressed by:
$$\frac{4}{3}\text{Al}(l) + \text{O}_2(g) \to \frac{2}{3}\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3(s), \quad \Delta G_1^\circ = -1060 + 0.21\,T\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$
$$2\text{Mg}(g) + \text{O}_2(g) \to 2\text{MgO}(s), \quad \Delta G_2^\circ = -1270 + 0.35\,T\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$
At what temperature does the thermodynamic feasibility invert, such that metallic aluminium can spontaneously reduce magnesium oxide ($\text{MgO}$) to gaseous magnesium?
questions.explanation: Step 1: The reduction of $\text{MgO}$ by $\text{Al}$ is represented by: $2\text{MgO}(s) + \frac{4}{3}\text{Al}(l) \to 2\text{Mg}(g) + \frac{2}{3}\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3(s)$. Step 2: The standard free energy change is $\Delta G_{\text{rxn}}^\circ = \Delta G_1^\circ - \Delta G_2^\circ = (-1060 + 0.21\,T) - (-1270 + 0.35\,T) = 210 - 0.14\,T\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$. Step 3: For the reduction to be spontaneous, $\Delta G_{\text{rxn}}^\circ \le 0$, which implies $210 - 0.14\,T \le 0$. Solving for temperature: $T \ge \frac{210}{0.14} = 1500\text{ K}$. Below $1500\text{ K}$, magnesium reduces alumina; above $1500\text{ K}$, aluminium spontaneously reduces magnesia. Distractor A results from confusing standard intercepts, distractor B is merely the boiling point of magnesium, and distractor C arises from an arithmetic mistake in the difference of slopes ($0.35 - 0.21 = 0.14$).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: In Mond's vapor-phase refining of nickel, impure nickel is reacted with carbon monoxide to form volatile nickel tetracarbonyl: $\text{Ni}(s) + 4\text{CO}(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{Ni}(\text{CO})_4(g)$. The standard enthalpy and entropy changes for this reaction are $\Delta H^\circ = -160.0\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ and $\Delta S^\circ = -400.0\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}$ (assumed independent of temperature). Calculate the equilibrium transition temperature at which $\Delta G^\circ = 0$, and predict the effect of increasing total pressure on the equilibrium yield of $\text{Ni}(\text{CO})_4$.
options: A) $400\text{ K}$; increasing pressure shifts equilibrium toward $\text{Ni}(\text{CO})_4$ formation
B) $400\text{ K}$; increasing pressure shifts equilibrium toward $\text{Ni}$ decomposition
C) $250\text{ K}$; increasing pressure shifts equilibrium toward $\text{Ni}(\text{CO})_4$ formation
D) $500\text{ K}$; increasing pressure has no effect on the equilibrium position
questions.explanation: Step 1: Setting $\Delta G^\circ = \Delta H^\circ - T\Delta S^\circ = 0$ yields $T = \frac{\Delta H^\circ}{\Delta S^\circ}$. Substituting the thermodynamic values: $T = \frac{-160.0 \times 10^3\text{ J mol}^{-1}}{-400.0\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}} = 400\text{ K}$. Below $400\text{ K}$, $\Delta G^\circ < 0$ and nickel carbonyl forms spontaneously; above $400\text{ K}$, $\Delta G^\circ > 0$ and it decomposes into pure nickel. Step 2: Applying Le Chatelier's principle, the forward reaction converts $4\text{ moles}$ of gas into $1\text{ mole}$ of gas ($\Delta n_g = 1 - 4 = -3 < 0$). Hence, increasing total pressure shifts the equilibrium in the forward direction, favoring $\text{Ni}(\text{CO})_4$ formation. Distractor B incorrectly predicts pressure response, while distractors C and D stem from conversion errors between kilojoules and joules.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: In the differential froth flotation of a complex sulfide ore containing galena ($\text{PbS}$) and sphalerite ($\text{ZnS}$), sodium cyanide ($\text{NaCN}$) and sodium ethyl xanthate are added. Which of the following chemical explanations accurately accounts for the depression of $\text{ZnS}$ while allowing $\text{PbS}$ to float in the froth?
options: A) $\text{NaCN}$ oxidizes $\text{PbS}$ to soluble $\text{Pb(CN)}_2$, leaving $\text{ZnS}$ hydrophobic

B) $\text{NaCN}$ forms a soluble coordination complex $[\text{Zn}(\text{CN})_4]^{2-}$ on the surface of $\text{ZnS}$, preventing xanthate collector adsorption, while $\text{PbS}$ adsorbs xanthate and floats
C) $\text{NaCN}$ selectively reduces $\text{ZnS}$ to metallic zinc which sinks due to high density
D) $\text{NaCN}$ acts as a frothing stabilizer that preferentially lowers the surface tension of water around $\text{PbS}$ particles
questions.explanation: Step 1: Sodium cyanide acts as a chemical depressant for $\text{ZnS}$. Cyanide ions react selectively with zinc sulfide particles at the mineral-water interface to form the highly stable, water-soluble complex tetracyanozincate(II): $\text{ZnS}(s) + 4\text{CN}^-(aq) \rightleftharpoons [\text{Zn}(\text{CN})_4]^{2-}(aq) + \text{S}^{2-}(aq)$. Step 2: Because the surface of $\text{ZnS}$ is masked by this hydrophilic ionic layer, the hydrocarbon tails of sodium ethyl xanthate collectors cannot chemisorb onto $\text{ZnS}$, preventing it from becoming water-repellent. Step 3: In contrast, $\text{PbS}$ does not form a stable cyanide complex under these conditions; xanthate anions bind to surface $\text{Pb}^{2+}$ ions, imparting strong hydrophobicity so that $\text{PbS}$ particles attach to ascending air bubbles and float. Distractor A reverses the metals, distractor C describes an impossible redox reduction, and distractor D confuses depressants with frothers.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: In the pyrometallurgical extraction of lead from galena ($\text{PbS}$) via self-reduction, concentrated ore is partially roasted to lead(II) oxide ($\text{PbO}$), and the air blast is subsequently stopped while heating continues so that unroasted $\text{PbS}$ reacts with $\text{PbO}$ to produce metallic lead. To convert all lead into metallic lead with zero residual sulfide or oxide, what is the stoichiometric mole ratio of unroasted $\text{PbS}$ to $\text{PbO}$ in the self-reduction step, and what is the theoretical yield of $\text{Pb}$ from $60.0\text{ mol}$ of initial $\text{PbS}$?
options: A) $1 : 1\text{ mole ratio, yielding } 30.0\text{ mol of } \text{Pb}$
B) $2 : 1\text{ mole ratio, yielding } 40.0\text{ mol of } \text{Pb}$
C) $1 : 3\text{ mole ratio, yielding } 45.0\text{ mol of } \text{Pb}$
D) $1 : 2\text{ mole ratio, yielding } 60.0\text{ mol of } \text{Pb}$
questions.explanation: Step 1: Write the self-reduction equation: $\text{PbS} + 2\text{PbO} \to 3\text{Pb} + \text{SO}_2$. The stoichiometric ratio of unroasted sulfide to oxide reactant is strictly $1 : 2$. Step 2: From an initial batch of $60.0\text{ mol}$ of $\text{PbS}$, two-thirds ($40.0\text{ mol}$) is roasted to $\text{PbO}$ according to $2\text{PbS} + 3\text{O}_2 \to 2\text{PbO} + 2\text{SO}_2$, yielding $40.0\text{ mol}$ of $\text{PbO}$. Step 3: The remaining one-third ($20.0\text{ mol}$) of unroasted $\text{PbS}$ reacts with the $40.0\text{ mol}$ of $\text{PbO}$ in a $1 : 2$ ratio to yield $3 \times 20.0 = 60.0\text{ mol}$ of metallic lead. Thus, all $60.0\text{ mol}$ of lead atoms originally present in the galena are recovered as metallic lead. Distractor A assumes an incorrect 1:1 stoichiometry, distractor B inverts the mole ratio, and distractor C assumes a 1:3 ratio.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: Zone refining is widely employed to produce ultra-high purity semiconductor-grade germanium. The segregation efficiency depends on the equilibrium partition coefficient $k = C_S / C_L$, where $C_S$ and $C_L$ are the impurity concentrations in the freezing solid and molten zone, respectively. If an ingot has an initially uniform antimony impurity concentration of $C_0 = 800\text{ ppm}$ and the partition coefficient of antimony in germanium is $k = 0.25$, determine the impurity concentration in the very first solid increment crystallized at the beginning of the ingot, and identify the direction in which the impurity migrates relative to heater movement.
options: A) $800\text{ ppm}$; impurities move opposite to the heater direction
B) $400\text{ ppm}$; impurities remain stationary in the solid matrix
C) $200\text{ ppm}$; impurities travel in the same direction as the molten zone
D) $3200\text{ ppm}$; impurities travel in the same direction as the molten zone
questions.explanation: Step 1: By definition of the partition coefficient, the concentration of solute freezing into the solid phase at the very beginning of the first pass ($x = 0$) is $C_S(0) = k \cdot C_0$. Step 2: Substituting $k = 0.25$ and $C_0 = 800\text{ ppm}$ gives: $C_S(0) = 0.25 \times 800\text{ ppm} = 200\text{ ppm}$. Step 3: Because $k < 1$, the impurity is more soluble in the molten liquid phase ($C_L = C_S / k = 4 C_S$) than in the solid phase. As the circular heater moves along the rod, the molten zone carries the rejected impurity forward, accumulating it at the terminal trailing end of the ingot. Distractor A assumes no purification ($k=1$), distractor B uses an erroneous partition factor of $0.50$, and distractor D divides by $k$ instead of multiplying.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: In the lower region of a blast furnace, solid coke reacts endothermically with carbon dioxide to produce carbon monoxide according to the Boudouard equilibrium: $\text{C}(s) + \text{CO}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{CO}(g)$. The standard reaction enthalpy and entropy changes are $\Delta H^\circ = +171.0\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ and $\Delta S^\circ = +180.0\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}$ (assumed independent of temperature). Calculate the temperature in Kelvin at which the standard equilibrium constant $K_p$ equals $1.0$.
questions.explanation: Step 1: The standard equilibrium constant is related to the standard Gibbs free energy change by $\Delta G^\circ = -RT \ln K_p$. When $K_p = 1.0$, $\ln(1.0) = 0$, so $\Delta G^\circ = 0$. Step 2: Substituting the thermodynamic relation $\Delta G^\circ = \Delta H^\circ - T\Delta S^\circ = 0$, we get $T = \frac{\Delta H^\circ}{\Delta S^\circ}$. Step 3: Convert enthalpy to joules: $\Delta H^\circ = 171.0 \times 10^3\text{ J mol}^{-1}$. Step 4: Solving for temperature: $T = \frac{171000\text{ J mol}^{-1}}{180.0\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}} = 950\text{ K}$. Hence, the required integer temperature is 950.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
To precipitate all silver from an aqueous cyanide solution containing exactly $0.40\text{ mol}$ of sodium dicyanoargentate(I), $\text{Na}[\text{Ag}(\text{CN})_2]$, pure zinc dust is added according to the displacement reaction:
$$2[\text{Ag}(\text{CN})_2]^-(aq) + \text{Zn}(s) \to [\text{Zn}(\text{CN})_4]^{2-}(aq) + 2\text{Ag}(s)$$
Taking the atomic mass of zinc as $65\text{ g mol}^{-1}$, calculate the minimum stoichiometric mass of zinc dust required in grams.
questions.explanation: Step 1: From the balanced ionic equation, $2\text{ moles}$ of $[\text{Ag}(\text{CN})_2]^-$ react with $1\text{ mole}$ of $\text{Zn}(s)$. Step 2: Determine moles of zinc required for $0.40\text{ mol}$ of complex: $n(\text{Zn}) = \frac{0.40}{2} = 0.20\text{ mol}$. Step 3: Calculate the mass of zinc: $m(\text{Zn}) = n(\text{Zn}) \times M(\text{Zn}) = 0.20\text{ mol} \times 65\text{ g mol}^{-1} = 13\text{ g}$. Thus, the final integer answer is 13.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: A steady electric current of $96.5\text{ A}$ is passed through a molten alumina-cryolite bath in an electrolytic cell for exactly $5.0\text{ hours}$ ($18000\text{ s}$). If the actual mass of pure aluminium deposited at the cathode is measured to be $121.5\text{ g}$, determine the percentage current efficiency of the cell. (Take Faraday's constant as $1\text{ F} = 96500\text{ C mol}^{-1}$ and atomic mass of aluminium as $27.0\text{ g mol}^{-1}$).
questions.explanation: Step 1: Calculate total electric charge passed through the cell: $Q = I \times t = 96.5\text{ A} \times 18000\text{ s} = 1737000\text{ C}$. Step 2: Calculate moles of electrons supplied: $n(e^-) = \frac{1737000\text{ C}}{96500\text{ C mol}^{-1}} = 18.0\text{ mol of } e^-$. Step 3: Cathode half-reaction is $\text{Al}^{3+} + 3e^- \to \text{Al}(l)$, requiring $3\text{ moles of } e^-$ per mole of $\text{Al}$. Theoretical moles of $\text{Al} = \frac{18.0}{3} = 6.0\text{ mol}$. Step 4: Theoretical mass of aluminium deposited is $m_{\text{theor}} = 6.0\text{ mol} \times 27.0\text{ g mol}^{-1} = 162.0\text{ g}$. Step 5: Current efficiency is: $\eta = \frac{m_{\text{actual}}}{m_{\text{theor}}} \times 100\% = \frac{121.5\text{ g}}{162.0\text{ g}} \times 100\% = 75\%$. Hence, the integer answer is 75.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: In the Ellingham diagram plotting standard Gibbs free energy of oxidation ($\Delta G^\circ$) against temperature ($T$) for the formation of magnesium oxide, $2\text{Mg} + \text{O}_2(g) \to 2\text{MgO}(s)$, the slope $\frac{d(\Delta G^\circ)}{dT}$ undergoes an abrupt upward increase at $1390\text{ K}$. Which of the following thermodynamic deductions correctly explains this phenomenon?
options: A) Magnesium boils at $1390\text{ K}$, changing reactants from liquid to gas and making $\Delta S^\circ$ significantly more negative, which sharply steepens the slope $-\Delta S^\circ$
B) Magnesium oxide sublimes at $1390\text{ K}$, creating extra gaseous product molecules
C) Magnesium undergoes a solid-state polymorphic phase transition with zero change in volume
D) Formation of magnesium peroxide ($\text{MgO}_2$) begins at $1390\text{ K}$
questions.explanation: Step 1: In an Ellingham diagram, the slope of any oxidation curve is given by $\frac{d(\Delta G^\circ)}{dT} = -\Delta S^\circ$. Step 2: Below $1390\text{ K}$, magnesium is liquid: $2\text{Mg}(l) + \text{O}_2(g) \to 2\text{MgO}(s)$, where the net change in moles of gas is $\Delta n_g = 0 - 1 = -1$. Step 3: At $1390\text{ K}$, magnesium boils into gas: $2\text{Mg}(g) + \text{O}_2(g) \to 2\text{MgO}(s)$, where three moles of gas condense into solid ($\Delta n_g = 0 - 3 = -3$). This makes $\Delta S^\circ$ substantially more negative. Step 4: Because the slope equals $-\Delta S^\circ$, a more negative entropy change causes a sharp increase in the positive slope of the line. Distractor B is incorrect because $\text{MgO}$ has an extremely high boiling point ($> 3000\text{ K}$), distractor C is incorrect because polymorphic phase transitions cause negligible entropy changes, and distractor D describes an unobserved oxidation state under pyrometallurgical conditions.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
In the reduction of wüstite ($\text{FeO}$) within a blast furnace, carbon monoxide ($\text{CO}$) and solid carbon ($\text{C}$) compete as reducing agents according to the reactions:
$$\text{FeO}(s) + \text{CO}(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{Fe}(s) + \text{CO}_2(g)$$
$$\text{FeO}(s) + \text{C}(s) \rightleftharpoons \text{Fe}(s) + \text{CO}(g)$$
Based on the intersection of the $\text{C}-\text{CO}$ and $\text{CO}-\text{CO}_2$ Ellingham lines at approximately $983\text{ K}$ ($710^\circ\text{C}$), which of the following statements correctly identifies the thermodynamically preferred reducing agent in the different temperature zones?
options: A) Below $983\text{ K}$, solid carbon is a better reducing agent than $\text{CO}$, whereas above $983\text{ K}$, $\text{CO}$ is superior
B) $\text{CO}$ is a more powerful reducing agent than solid carbon at all temperatures inside the blast furnace
C) Below $983\text{ K}$, $\text{CO}$ is thermodynamically a better reducing agent than solid carbon, whereas above $983\text{ K}$, solid carbon is the more effective reducing agent
D) Solid carbon reduces $\text{FeO}$ only when liquid iron dissolves dissolved oxygen at $1800\text{ K}$
questions.explanation: Step 1: In the Ellingham diagram, the line for $2\text{CO} + \text{O}_2 \to 2\text{CO}_2$ has a positive slope ($\Delta S^\circ < 0$), while the line for $2\text{C} + \text{O}_2 \to 2\text{CO}$ has a negative slope ($\Delta S^\circ > 0$). Step 2: These two lines intersect at $T \approx 983\text{ K}$ ($710^\circ\text{C}$). Below $983\text{ K}$, the $\text{CO} \to \text{CO}_2$ line lies lower than the $\text{C} \to \text{CO}$ line, meaning $\text{CO}$ has a greater affinity for oxygen and $\Delta G^\circ$ for reduction by $\text{CO}$ is more negative. Step 3: Above $983\text{ K}$, the downward-sloping $\text{C} \to \text{CO}$ line falls below the $\text{CO} \to \text{CO}_2$ line and below the $\text{Fe} \to \text{FeO}$ line, making solid carbon the thermodynamically favored reducing agent. Distractor A inverts the two temperature regimes, distractor B ignores the Boudouard temperature dependence, and distractor D misrepresents dissolved oxygen kinetics.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: During the smelting of copper in a reverberatory furnace and subsequent Bessemerization, copper matte (a mixture of $\text{Cu}_2\text{S}$ and $\text{FeS}$) is charged into a silica-lined Bessemer converter with an air blast. What is the fundamental chemical role of the silica ($\text{SiO}_2$) lining/flux, and how is iron selectively removed before copper is reduced?
options: A) Silica reduces cuprous oxide to metallic copper before iron sulfide can react

B) Silica acts as an acidic flux that selectively binds basic ferrous oxide ($\text{FeO}$) into a lighter fusible slag ($\text{FeSiO}_3$), allowing complete removal of iron prior to copper auto-reduction
C) Silica lining decomposes to elemental silicon which alloys with copper to form bronze
D) Silica reacts with sulfur dioxide to prevent bubble formation in blister copper
questions.explanation: Step 1: Iron has a much higher thermodynamic affinity for oxygen than copper ($\Delta G_f^\circ$ of $\text{FeO}$ is far more negative than that of $\text{Cu}_2\text{O}$). Therefore, upon blowing air, $\text{FeS}$ oxidizes first: $2\text{FeS} + 3\text{O}_2 \to 2\text{FeO} + 2\text{SO}_2$. Step 2: The basic gangue oxide $\text{FeO}$ immediately reacts with the acidic silica flux/lining according to: $\text{FeO}(s) + \text{SiO}_2(s) \to \text{FeSiO}_3(l)$. Step 3: Ferrous silicate ($\text{FeSiO}_3$) forms a lighter, immiscible molten slag that floats on top of the copper matte and is periodically tapped off. Only after virtually all iron has been slagged off does the partial oxidation of $\text{Cu}_2\text{S}$ and self-reduction to metallic copper proceed. Distractor A confuses fluxing with reduction, distractor C describes bronze manufacture, and distractor D misidentifies the cause of blisters.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: Low-grade copper ores containing oxidized or sulfide minerals are economically extracted via hydrometallurgy by leaching with dilute sulfuric acid to generate aqueous $\text{CuSO}_4$, followed by cementation with scrap iron: $\text{Cu}^{2+}(aq) + \text{Fe}(s) \to \text{Cu}(s) + \text{Fe}^{2+}(aq)$. Although reduction of $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ by hydrogen gas ($\text{Cu}^{2+} + \text{H}_2 \to \text{Cu} + 2\text{H}^+$) has a favorable standard potential ($E^\circ = +0.34\text{ V}$), why is scrap iron preferred industrially?
options: A) Reduction by scrap iron has a negative cell potential and requires an external battery
B) Hydrogen gas cannot reduce $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ ions under any thermodynamic conditions
C) Scrap iron forms an insoluble $\text{Fe-Cu}$ alloy precipitate that requires no filtration

D) Although $\text{H}_2$ reduction ($\text{Cu}^{2+} + \text{H}_2 \to \text{Cu} + 2\text{H}^+$) is spontaneous, it requires expensive pressurized autoclaves and catalysts, whereas scrap iron operates rapidly under ambient temperature and pressure at low cost
questions.explanation: Step 1: The reduction of $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ by $\text{Fe}$ has $E_{\text{cell}}^\circ = E^\circ(\text{Cu}^{2+}/\text{Cu}) - E^\circ(\text{Fe}^{2+}/\text{Fe}) = +0.34 - (-0.44) = +0.78\text{ V} > 0$, making $\Delta G^\circ = -2 \times 96500 \times 0.78 = -150.5\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ (highly spontaneous). Step 2: The reduction by $\text{H}_2$ also has $E_{\text{cell}}^\circ = +0.34 - 0.00 = +0.34\text{ V} > 0$ and is thermodynamically spontaneous. Step 3: However, molecular $\text{H}_2$ has a high $\text{H}-\text{H}$ bond dissociation energy ($436\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$) and very slow reaction kinetics at ambient temperature, requiring high-pressure autoclaves ($20-30\text{ bar}$), elevated temperatures ($150-200^\circ\text{C}$), and expensive catalysts. In contrast, scrap iron is cheap, widely available, and reduces copper rapidly under ambient conditions. Distractor A falsely claims the iron reaction is non-spontaneous, distractor B denies thermodynamic feasibility of $\text{H}_2$ reduction, and distractor C is incorrect because copper precipitates as pure metallic powder, not an alloy.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: In the Van Arkel-de Boer process for the ultra-purification of zirconium or titanium, crude metal is treated with iodine in an evacuated vessel at $523\text{ K}$ and subsequently decomposed on a tungsten filament at $1800\text{ K}$: $\text{Zr}(s) + 2\text{I}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{ZrI}_4(g)$. Which of the following thermodynamic rationales correctly explains the operation of this process?
options: A) Formation of $\text{ZrI}_4$ is exothermic ($\Delta H^\circ < 0$) and favored at $523\text{ K}$, while its thermal decomposition on the hot filament is endothermic ($\Delta H^\circ > 0$) and driven by high temperature ($1800\text{ K}$)
B) Formation of $\text{ZrI}_4$ is endothermic and occurs on the hot filament, depositing pure zirconium on the vessel walls
C) Iodine acts as an oxidizing flux that converts oxygen and nitrogen impurities into volatile iodides
D) The tungsten filament reacts chemically with $\text{ZrI}_4$ to form a tungsten-zirconium intermetallic complex
questions.explanation: Step 1: The direct iodination of zirconium: $\text{Zr}(s) + 2\text{I}_2(g) \to \text{ZrI}_4(g)$ is an exothermic synthesis reaction ($\Delta H^\circ < 0$). By Le Chatelier's principle, it is thermodynamically favored at moderate temperatures ($523\text{ K}$). Step 2: The reverse reaction: $\text{ZrI}_4(g) \to \text{Zr}(s) + 2\text{I}_2(g)$ is an endothermic bond-breaking dissociation ($\Delta H^\circ > 0$) with a positive entropy change ($\Delta S^\circ > 0$, since 1 mole of gas produces solid plus 2 moles of gas). Step 3: At $1800\text{ K}$ on the electrically heated tungsten filament, the $T\Delta S^\circ$ term dominates, making $\Delta G^\circ$ for decomposition negative. Zirconium deposits onto the tungsten wire as pure metal, while liberated iodine vapor diffuses back to react with crude metal. Distractor B reverses the temperature locations, distractor C falsely claims impurities volatilize, and distractor D incorrectly posits an intermetallic alloy reaction.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: During the electrolytic refining of blister copper using an acidified aqueous $\text{CuSO}_4$ bath, crude copper acts as the anode while pure copper acts as the cathode. What is the correct behavioral description of electropositive impurities (such as $\text{Fe}, \text{Ni}, \text{Zn}$) and noble impurities (such as $\text{Ag}, \text{Au}, \text{Pt}$) present in the blister anode?
options: A) $\text{Ag}$ and $\text{Au}$ dissolve into the electrolyte and deposit along with copper at the cathode
B) $\text{Fe}$ and $\text{Ni}$ dissolve into the electrolyte as cations and remain in solution, while less electropositive noble metals ($\text{Ag}, \text{Au}$) settle undissolved as anode mud
C) All impurities are converted into volatile hydrides that escape with electrolytic gases
D) $\text{Zn}$ and $\text{Ni}$ precipitate as insoluble oxides on the cathode surface
questions.explanation: Step 1: Compare standard reduction potentials: $E^\circ(\text{Zn}^{2+}/\text{Zn}) = -0.76\text{ V}$, $E^\circ(\text{Fe}^{2+}/\text{Fe}) = -0.44\text{ V}$, $E^\circ(\text{Ni}^{2+}/\text{Ni}) = -0.25\text{ V}$, $E^\circ(\text{Cu}^{2+}/\text{Cu}) = +0.34\text{ V}$, $E^\circ(\text{Ag}^+/\text{Ag}) = +0.80\text{ V}$, $E^\circ(\text{Au}^{3+}/\text{Au}) = +1.50\text{ V}$. Step 2: Because $\text{Fe}, \text{Ni}, \text{Zn}$ have more negative reduction potentials than copper, they oxidize more easily at the anode and enter the electrolyte as $\text{Fe}^{2+}, \text{Ni}^{2+}, \text{Zn}^{2+}$. However, at the cathode, $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ has a much higher reduction potential, so only $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ ions discharge, leaving $\text{Fe}^{2+}, \text{Ni}^{2+}, \text{Zn}^{2+}$ dissolved in solution. Step 3: Noble metals ($\text{Ag}, \text{Au}, \text{Pt}$) have higher reduction potentials than copper, so they cannot be oxidized at the operating anode potential and drop to the bottom of the cell as valuable anode mud. Distractor A contradicts electrode potentials, distractor C describes hydride generation, and distractor D posits an impossible cathodic precipitation.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: In the industrial electrometallurgy of aluminium (Hall-Héroult process), pure alumina ($\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$) is not electrolyzed alone. Instead, cryolite ($\text{Na}_3\text{AlF}_6$) and fluorspar ($\text{CaF}_2$) are mixed with alumina. Which of the following statements comprehensively explains the three essential physicochemical functions of this molten fluoride electrolyte mixture?
options: A) They act as chemical reducing agents to donate electrons to aluminium ions
B) They increase the melting point of the bath to ensure complete vaporization of sodium

C) They lower the melting point of alumina from $2050^\circ\text{C}$ to $\sim 950^\circ\text{C}$, enhance electrical conductivity of the melt, and lower the bath density so that liquid aluminium collects safely at the bottom
D) They suppress the evolution of carbon dioxide gas at the graphite anodes
questions.explanation: Step 1: Pure $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ has an exceedingly high melting point of $\sim 2050^\circ\text{C}$ and poor electrical conductivity in the molten state. Dissolving alumina in a eutectic mixture of cryolite ($\text{Na}_3\text{AlF}_6$) and fluorspar ($\text{CaF}_2$) depresses the operating melting point to $\sim 950^\circ\text{C}$, substantially reducing electrical energy consumption. Step 2: The dissociation into mobile $\text{Na}^+, \text{Ca}^{2+}, \text{AlF}_6^{3-}$, and $\text{F}^-$ ions provides high ionic conductivity to the electrolyte. Step 3: Crucially, the density of the molten fluoride bath ($\sim 2.1\text{ g cm}^{-3}$) is lower than that of molten aluminium ($\sim 2.3\text{ g cm}^{-3}$) at $950^\circ\text{C}$. This density difference ensures that liquid aluminium sinks to the bottom of the electrolytic cell, where it is shielded from re-oxidation by atmospheric air and anode gases. Distractor A is false because electric current reduces aluminium, distractor B inverts the melting point effect, and distractor D is contradicted by anode gas composition.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: When bauxite ore contains silica ($\text{SiO}_2$) as the predominant gangue impurity, Bayer's process suffers significant losses of alumina and caustic soda due to insoluble sodium aluminium silicate precipitation. In such cases, Serpeck's process is employed. Which of the following reaction sequences accurately represents the chemistry of Serpeck's process?
options: A) Silica is converted into sodium silicate while alumina is reduced to metallic aluminium
B) Nitrogen gas oxidizes iron impurities to magnetic $\text{Fe}_3\text{O}_4$
C) Silica reacts with nitrogen to form volatile silicon tetrachloride

D) Heating bauxite with coke in a nitrogen current converts alumina to $\text{AlN}$ while reducing silica to volatile silicon, after which $\text{AlN}$ is hydrolyzed to $\text{Al(OH)}_3$ yielding ammonia gas as a byproduct
questions.explanation: Step 1: In Serpeck's process, finely powdered siliceous bauxite is mixed with coke and heated to $1800^\circ\text{C}$ in a current of nitrogen gas: $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 + 3\text{C} + \text{N}_2 \to 2\text{AlN} + 3\text{CO}$. Step 2: Simultaneously, the silica gangue is reduced by carbon to elemental silicon, which volatilizes at this high temperature: $\text{SiO}_2 + 2\text{C} \to \text{Si}(g) + 2\text{CO}(g)$, thereby separating it from alumina. Step 3: The solid aluminium nitride ($\text{AlN}$) is then hydrolyzed with hot water or dilute alkali: $\text{AlN} + 3\text{H}_2\text{O} \to \text{Al(OH)}_3(s) + \text{NH}_3(g)$. Ammonia gas is recovered as a valuable commercial byproduct, and the precipitated $\text{Al(OH)}_3$ is calcined at $1200^\circ\text{C}$ to produce pure alumina ($\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$). Distractors A, B, and C describe fictitious reactions.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: In a single-pass zone refining operation, an ingot of length $L$ containing an initially uniform impurity concentration $C_0$ is traversed by a narrow molten zone of length $l$. The concentration profile of the impurity in the recrystallized solid is given by Pfann's relationship: $C(x) = C_0\left[1 - (1 - k)e^{-kx/l}\right]$, where $k$ is the equilibrium partition coefficient. If an ingot has $C_0 = 2000\text{ ppm}$ and the impurity has $k = 0.05$, determine the impurity concentration in the recrystallized solid at the starting edge ($x = 0$), and state where the rejected impurities concentrate.
options: A) $100\text{ ppm}$; impurities with $k < 1$ concentrate in the melt and travel toward the finishing end of the ingot
B) $1900\text{ ppm}$; impurities with $k < 1$ freeze preferentially in the initial solid
C) $2000\text{ ppm}$; single pass zone refining produces no change in impurity concentration
D) $40000\text{ ppm}$; impurities with $k < 1$ vaporize into the surrounding inert gas
questions.explanation: Step 1: Evaluate the concentration at the starting edge $x = 0$: $C(0) = C_0\left[1 - (1 - k)e^0\right] = C_0\left[1 - (1 - k)\right] = k \cdot C_0$. Step 2: Substituting $k = 0.05$ and $C_0 = 2000\text{ ppm}$: $C(0) = 0.05 \times 2000\text{ ppm} = 100\text{ ppm}$. This represents a 20-fold purification at the leading edge. Step 3: Because $k = C_S / C_L < 1$, the solute is more soluble in the molten zone than in the solid phase. As the heater moves along the ingot, impurities are continually swept along with the molten liquid and deposited at the terminal end of the bar, which is eventually cut off and discarded. Distractor B confuses $(1-k)$ with $k$, distractor C ignores segregation, and distractor D inverts the partition coefficient.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: In the Goldschmidt thermite process, chromium(III) oxide is reduced by aluminium powder according to: $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_3(s) + 2\text{Al}(s) \to 2\text{Cr}(l) + \text{Al}_2\text{O}_3(s)$. Given the standard enthalpies of formation: $\Delta H_f^\circ(\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_3) = -1140.0\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ and $\Delta H_f^\circ(\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3) = -1676.0\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$. Calculate the standard enthalpy change of the reaction ($\Delta H_{\text{rxn}}^\circ$) per mole of $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_3$ reduced, and explain why chromium is obtained in molten form.
options: A) $+536.0\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$; the reaction is endothermic and requires continuous external electrical heating
B) $-2816.0\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$; the reaction releases enough heat to vaporize both chromium and aluminium
C) $-536.0\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$; the reaction is highly exothermic and the intense heat liberated melts the reduced chromium metal ($T > 1900^\circ\text{C}$), allowing it to collect as a liquid ingot
D) $-268.0\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$; the reaction proceeds via solid-state diffusion without liquid formation
questions.explanation: Step 1: Applying Hess's law to calculate the standard reaction enthalpy: $\Delta H_{\text{rxn}}^\circ = \sum \Delta H_f^\circ(\text{products}) - \sum \Delta H_f^\circ(\text{reactants})$. Step 2: Since elemental aluminium and chromium in standard states have $\Delta H_f^\circ = 0$, we have: $\Delta H_{\text{rxn}}^\circ = \Delta H_f^\circ(\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3) - \Delta H_f^\circ(\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_3) = -1676.0 - (-1140.0) = -536.0\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$. Step 3: The immense release of $536\text{ kJ}$ per mole of $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_3$ rapidly raises the temperature of the charge beyond $2500^\circ\text{C}$, well above the melting point of chromium ($1857^\circ\text{C}$). The molten chromium settles to the bottom of the crucible beneath the molten alumina slag, facilitating straightforward mechanical separation upon cooling. Distractor A has an incorrect positive sign, distractor B adds the two enthalpies, and distractor D halves the reaction enthalpy.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: During the partial roasting of copper pyrites ($\text{CuFeS}_2$), iron sulfide ($\text{FeS}$) is selectively converted into iron(II) oxide ($\text{FeO}$) while copper sulfide ($\text{Cu}_2\text{S}$) remains unoxidized. Which of the following thermodynamic principles explains this selective oxidation behavior?
options: A) Cuprous sulfide has a lower melting point and sublimes before iron can react

B) Iron has a much higher thermodynamic affinity for oxygen than copper ($\Delta G^\circ$ for $\text{FeO}$ is far more negative than for $\text{Cu}_2\text{O}$), and unreacted $\text{FeS}$ readily reduces any $\text{Cu}_2\text{O}$ back to $\text{Cu}_2\text{S}$
C) Copper sulfide reacts with nitrogen from the air blast to form a protective copper nitride shell
D) Iron sulfide acts as a homogeneous catalyst for the thermal decomposition of sulfur dioxide
questions.explanation: Step 1: Comparing the Ellingham oxidation curves, the line for $2\text{Fe} + \text{O}_2 \to 2\text{FeO}$ lies substantially lower than the line for $4\text{Cu} + \text{O}_2 \to 2\text{Cu}_2\text{O}$. Consequently, the free energy change of oxidation for $\text{FeS}$ ($2\text{FeS} + 3\text{O}_2 \to 2\text{FeO} + 2\text{SO}_2$) is far more negative than that for $\text{Cu}_2\text{S}$ ($2\text{Cu}_2\text{S} + 3\text{O}_2 \to 2\text{Cu}_2\text{O} + 2\text{SO}_2$). Step 2: If any $\text{Cu}_2\text{O}$ is transiently formed, it immediately reacts with residual $\text{FeS}$ via the exchange reaction: $\text{Cu}_2\text{O} + \text{FeS} \to \text{Cu}_2\text{S} + \text{FeO}$, which has a strongly negative $\Delta G^\circ$. Thus, copper remains completely as $\text{Cu}_2\text{S}$ until all $\text{FeS}$ is oxidized and slagged off. Distractors A, C, and D propose unphysical chemical mechanisms.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: In the Kroll process for extracting metallic titanium, rutile ore ($\text{TiO}_2$) is first converted to titanium tetrachloride ($\text{TiCl}_4$) and then reduced with molten magnesium under an inert argon atmosphere: $\text{TiCl}_4(g) + 2\text{Mg}(l) \xrightarrow{1100\text{ K}, \text{Ar}} \text{Ti}(s) + 2\text{MgCl}_2(l)$. Why is direct carbothermic reduction of $\text{TiO}_2$ unfeasible, and why is an argon atmosphere strictly required during magnesium reduction?
options: A) Carbon reduces $\text{TiO}_2$ to titanium hydride, while nitrogen promotes grain growth
B) Carbon is too expensive industrially, and air facilitates oxidation of magnesium
C) Carbon reduction is too exothermic and causes explosive destruction of the furnace

D) Carbon reduction yields brittle, interstitial titanium carbide ($\text{TiC}$), while reduction of $\text{TiCl}_4$ with molten magnesium must be conducted under argon because hot titanium absorbs oxygen and nitrogen from air, causing extreme embrittlement
questions.explanation: Step 1: Attempting direct reduction of $\text{TiO}_2$ with carbon at high temperatures results in the formation of extremely stable interstitial titanium carbide rather than pure metal: $\text{TiO}_2 + 3\text{C} \to \text{TiC} + 2\text{CO}$. The resulting $\text{TiC}$ is refractory, brittle, and impossible to convert into ductile titanium. Step 2: In the Kroll process, carbo-chlorination generates covalent $\text{TiCl}_4$, which is purified by fractional distillation. Step 3: When $\text{TiCl}_4$ is reduced by molten $\text{Mg}$ at $850-900^\circ\text{C}$, the reaction must be shielded under an inert argon atmosphere because titanium at elevated temperatures is an exceptional getter for oxygen and nitrogen, forming solid solutions and nitrides ($\text{TiN}$) that render the titanium sponge irreversibly brittle. Distractors A, B, and C present incorrect chemical claims.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: Consider two specialized metallurgical refining operations: (1) Poling of molten copper in a reverberatory furnace, and (2) Cupellation of argentiferous lead. Which of the following statements correctly describes the underlying chemical principles of both operations?
options: A) Poling reduces cuprous oxide impurities via hydrocarbon gases from green wood, while cupellation separates silver by selectively oxidizing lead to litharge ($\text{PbO}$) which is absorbed by the porous bone-ash cupel
B) Poling removes iron as silicate slag, while cupellation utilizes mercury to form silver amalgam
C) Poling introduces carbon to increase the tensile strength of copper, while cupellation distills lead under vacuum
D) Poling electrolyzes blister copper in molten salt, while cupellation precipitates silver chloride
questions.explanation: Step 1: Poling: In blister copper refining, the molten metal contains residual copper(I) oxide ($\text{Cu}_2\text{O}$). Stirring with freshly cut green wood poles releases reducing gases (hydrocarbons such as methane $\text{CH}_4$, along with $\text{CO}$ and $\text{H}_2$), which reduce $\text{Cu}_2\text{O}$ back to metallic copper: $\text{CH}_4 + 4\text{Cu}_2\text{O} \to 8\text{Cu} + \text{CO}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$. Step 2: Cupellation: Argentiferous lead (lead containing silver impurity) is placed in an oval porous cupel made of bone ash or cement and heated in a blast of air. Lead oxidizes preferentially to litharge ($\text{PbO}$): $2\text{Pb} + \text{O}_2 \to 2\text{PbO}$. Molten $\text{PbO}$ is volatile and partially absorbed into the porous cupel walls, leaving behind a pure bead of unoxidized silver. Distractor B confuses poling with smelting and cupellation with amalgamation, distractor C confuses poling with carburization of steel, and distractor D misidentifies electrochemical processes.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: A polymetallic sulfide ore containing galena ($\text{PbS}$), sphalerite ($\text{ZnS}$), and pyrite ($\text{FeS}_2$) is processed by differential froth flotation. In the first flotation stage, sodium cyanide ($\text{NaCN}$) and sodium ethyl xanthate are added. In the second stage, copper sulfate ($\text{CuSO}_4$) is added to the pulp. Which of the following statements accurately describes the chemical roles of $\text{NaCN}$ and $\text{CuSO}_4$ across these stages?
options: A) $\text{CuSO}_4$ depresses galena, while $\text{NaCN}$ activates pyrite

B) $\text{NaCN}$ depresses $\text{ZnS}$ and $\text{FeS}_2$ by surface complexation while $\text{PbS}$ floats with xanthate; addition of $\text{CuSO}_4$ subsequently reactivates $\text{ZnS}$ by forming a $\text{CuS}$ surface coating that binds collector
C) $\text{NaCN}$ oxidizes sulfide ions to sulfate, while $\text{CuSO}_4$ acts as a frothing agent
D) Both $\text{NaCN}$ and $\text{CuSO}_4$ act as non-selective collectors that float all sulfides simultaneously
questions.explanation: Step 1: In the first stage, $\text{NaCN}$ is added as a depressant. Cyanide ions form soluble anionic cyano-complexes $[\text{Zn}(\text{CN})_4]^{2-}$ and $[\text{Fe}(\text{CN})_6]^{4-}$ on the surfaces of $\text{ZnS}$ and $\text{FeS}_2$, rendering them hydrophilic and preventing xanthate collector adsorption. Galena ($\text{PbS}$) does not form stable cyanide complexes and is floated selectively. Step 2: In the second stage, $\text{CuSO}_4$ is added to the tailings as an activator. Copper(II) ions undergo an exchange reaction with surface zinc ions: $\text{ZnS}(s) + \text{Cu}^{2+}(aq) \to \text{CuS}(s) + \text{Zn}^{2+}(aq)$. Step 3: The thin surface layer of copper sulfide ($\text{CuS}$) readily adsorbs ethyl xanthate collectors, allowing $\text{ZnS}$ to be recovered in the second froth. Pyrite remains depressed until the medium is acidified in a third stage. Distractor A reverses the roles, distractor C posits an irrelevant redox reaction, and distractor D ignores differential flotation selectivity.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: Carbo-chlorination is an indispensable extractive technique used to convert refractory oxides (such as $\text{TiO}_2$ and $\text{ZrO}_2$) into volatile anhydrous chlorides: $\text{TiO}_2(s) + 2\text{C}(s) + 2\text{Cl}_2(g) \to \text{TiCl}_4(g) + 2\text{CO}(g)$. Why cannot rutile be chlorinated simply by passing $\text{Cl}_2$ gas alone over heated $\text{TiO}_2$, and what thermodynamic advantage does the addition of carbon provide?
options: A) Carbo-chlorination produces solid titanium trichloride that precipitates without heating
B) Direct chlorination with chlorine gas alone is highly explosive at ambient temperature

C) Direct chlorination is thermodynamically unfeasible ($\Delta G^\circ > 0$), but coupling with carbon oxidation provides a strong negative $\Delta G^\circ$ driving force and yields volatile $\text{TiCl}_4$ that can be fractionally distilled to remove impurities
D) Rutile ore dissolves in liquid chlorine to form an aqueous coordination complex
questions.explanation: Step 1: Direct chlorination of rutile: $\text{TiO}_2(s) + 2\text{Cl}_2(g) \to \text{TiCl}_4(g) + \text{O}_2(g)$ has a positive standard Gibbs free energy change ($\Delta G^\circ > 0$, approximately $+160\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ at $1000\text{ K}$) because the $\text{Ti}-\text{O}$ bond in rutile is exceptionally strong. Hence, chlorine alone cannot react with $\text{TiO}_2$. Step 2: The oxidation of carbon to carbon monoxide: $2\text{C}(s) + \text{O}_2(g) \to 2\text{CO}(g)$ is strongly exergonic ($\Delta G^\circ \approx -400\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ at $1000\text{ K}$). Step 3: Coupling these two reactions yields the net carbo-chlorination reaction with $\Delta G_{\text{net}}^\circ = +160 + (-400) = -240\text{ kJ mol}^{-1} \ll 0$. The chemical drive to form stable $\text{CO}$ makes the process thermodynamically spontaneous. Furthermore, volatile $\text{TiCl}_4$ (b.p. $136^\circ\text{C}$) boils off and is readily purified from non-volatile gangue chlorides by fractional distillation. Distractor A is chemically incorrect, distractor B is contrary to the unreactive nature of $\text{TiO}_2$, and distractor D is unphysical.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: Liquation and distillation are physical refining techniques based on differences in phase change temperatures between the extracted metal and its accompanying impurities. Which of the following pairs of metals correctly exemplifies the appropriate application of liquation and distillation refining, respectively?
options: A) Liquation refines zinc from iron; distillation refines copper from silver
B) Liquation refines titanium from oxygen; distillation refines aluminium from silicon
C) Liquation refines nickel from cobalt; distillation refines iron from silica

D) Liquation refines low-melting metals like tin ($\text{Sn}$) and bismuth ($\text{Bi}$) from high-melting impurities, while distillation refines volatile metals like zinc ($\text{Zn}$) and mercury ($\text{Hg}$) from non-volatile impurities
questions.explanation: Step 1: Liquation is used when the metal has a substantially lower melting point than its impurities. The crude metal is placed on the sloping hearth of a reverberatory furnace heated just above the metal's melting point. The metal melts and flows down the hearth, leaving behind unmelted high-melting impurities. This process is ideally suited for tin ($\text{Sn}$, m.p. $232^\circ\text{C}$, separated from iron and copper impurities) and bismuth ($\text{Bi}$, m.p. $271^\circ\text{C}$). Step 2: Distillation is employed when the metal has a low boiling point and impurities are non-volatile. Heating the crude metal vaporizes the metal, and the vapor is condensed in a separate receiver. This technique is used for zinc ($\text{Zn}$, b.p. $907^\circ\text{C}$, separated from lead and iron), cadmium ($\text{Cd}$, b.p. $767^\circ\text{C}$), and mercury ($\text{Hg}$, b.p. $357^\circ\text{C}$). Distractors A, B, and C pair metals with refining techniques that do not correspond to their physical properties.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
A smelting furnace is charged with $100\text{ mol}$ of chalcopyrite ore ($\text{CuFeS}_2$). During roasting and smelting in the presence of excess silica flux, all the iron present in the ore is converted into iron(II) silicate slag ($\text{FeSiO}_3$) according to:
$$2\text{CuFeS}_2 + \text{O}_2 \to \text{Cu}_2\text{S} + 2\text{FeS} + \text{SO}_2$$
$$2\text{FeS} + 3\text{O}_2 \to 2\text{FeO} + 2\text{SO}_2$$
$$\text{FeO} + \text{SiO}_2 \to \text{FeSiO}_3$$
Assuming complete quantitative conversion of iron, calculate the total number of moles of $\text{FeSiO}_3$ slag produced.
questions.explanation: Step 1: From the formula $\text{CuFeS}_2$, each mole of chalcopyrite contains exactly one mole of iron atoms. Therefore, $100\text{ mol}$ of $\text{CuFeS}_2$ contains $100\text{ mol}$ of iron. Step 2: In the initial roasting stage, $2\text{ mol } \text{CuFeS}_2$ yields $2\text{ mol } \text{FeS}$, so $100\text{ mol}$ of $\text{FeS}$ is formed. Step 3: In the smelting stage, $100\text{ mol}$ of $\text{FeS}$ oxidizes to $100\text{ mol}$ of $\text{FeO}$. Step 4: The $100\text{ mol}$ of $\text{FeO}$ reacts with $100\text{ mol}$ of $\text{SiO}_2$ to produce exactly $100\text{ mol}$ of molten $\text{FeSiO}_3$ slag. Hence, the integer answer is 100.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
In a Van Arkel refining apparatus, exactly $1.0\text{ mol}$ of pure gaseous titanium tetraiodide ($\text{TiI}_4$) is completely decomposed on an electrically heated tungsten filament at $1800\text{ K}$ according to:
$$\text{TiI}_4(g) \to \text{Ti}(s) + 2\text{I}_2(g)$$
Taking the atomic mass of titanium as $48\text{ g mol}^{-1}$, calculate the mass of pure titanium metal deposited onto the tungsten filament in grams.
questions.explanation: Step 1: From the balanced dissociation reaction: $\text{TiI}_4(g) \to \text{Ti}(s) + 2\text{I}_2(g)$, the stoichiometric ratio between $\text{TiI}_4$ vapor and deposited metallic $\text{Ti}$ is $1 : 1$. Step 2: Complete thermal decomposition of $1.0\text{ mol}$ of $\text{TiI}_4$ yields $1.0\text{ mol}$ of elemental titanium. Step 3: Calculate the mass deposited: $m(\text{Ti}) = n(\text{Ti}) \times M(\text{Ti}) = 1.0\text{ mol} \times 48\text{ g mol}^{-1} = 48\text{ g}$. Hence, the final integer answer is 48.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: Zinc oxide is reduced by carbon in an industrial retort to produce zinc vapor and carbon monoxide: $\text{ZnO}(s) + \text{C}(s) \to \text{Zn}(g) + \text{CO}(g)$. The standard reaction enthalpy and standard reaction entropy changes are $\Delta H^\circ = +360.0\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ and $\Delta S^\circ = +300.0\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}$ (assumed temperature-independent). Calculate the minimum temperature in Kelvin above which this carbothermic reduction becomes thermodynamically spontaneous under standard pressure.
questions.explanation: Step 1: The condition for thermodynamic spontaneity is $\Delta G^\circ \le 0$. Setting $\Delta G^\circ = \Delta H^\circ - T\Delta S^\circ = 0$ yields the minimum threshold temperature: $T = \frac{\Delta H^\circ}{\Delta S^\circ}$. Step 2: Convert standard enthalpy to joules: $\Delta H^\circ = 360.0 \times 10^3\text{ J mol}^{-1} = 360000\text{ J mol}^{-1}$. Step 3: Compute temperature: $T = \frac{360000\text{ J mol}^{-1}}{300.0\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}} = 1200\text{ K}$. Above $1200\text{ K}$, the positive $T\Delta S^\circ$ term exceeds $\Delta H^\circ$, rendering $\Delta G^\circ$ negative. Hence, the integer answer is 1200.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: In a Hall-Héroult electrolytic cell operating at a constant current efficiency of $75\%$, exactly $108\text{ g}$ of pure aluminium is deposited at the cathode. Given that the reduction half-reaction is $\text{Al}^{3+} + 3e^- \to \text{Al}(l)$ and the atomic mass of aluminium is $27\text{ g mol}^{-1}$, calculate the total quantity of electric charge passed through the cell in Faradays ($1\text{ F} = 96500\text{ C mol}^{-1}$).
questions.explanation: Step 1: Calculate moles of aluminium deposited: $n(\text{Al}) = \frac{108\text{ g}}{27\text{ g mol}^{-1}} = 4.0\text{ mol}$. Step 2: From the cathode half-reaction $\text{Al}^{3+} + 3e^- \to \text{Al}$, $3\text{ moles of electrons}$ ($3\text{ Faradays}$) are required per mole of $\text{Al}$. Theoretical charge required: $Q_{\text{theor}} = 4.0 \times 3\text{ F} = 12\text{ F}$. Step 3: Account for the $75\%$ current efficiency: $\eta = \frac{Q_{\text{theor}}}{Q_{\text{actual}}} \implies Q_{\text{actual}} = \frac{12\text{ F}}{0.75} = 16\text{ F}$. Hence, the total charge passed is 16 Faradays, giving the integer answer 16.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: In an Ellingham diagram displaying standard Gibbs free energies of oxidation per mole of $\text{O}_2$ consumed ($\Delta G^\circ$ versus $T$) for various elements, the curves provide fundamental thermodynamic criteria for pyrometallurgical reductions. Which of the following thermodynamic deductions regarding these diagrams is/are correct?
options: A) For most metal oxidation curves $2M + \text{O}_2(g) \to 2MO(s)$, the slope $\frac{d(\Delta G^\circ)}{dT} = -\Delta S^\circ$ is positive because disordered gaseous oxygen is consumed to produce a condensed, ordered solid oxide, causing $\Delta S^\circ < 0$

B) When a metal reactant undergoes fusion (melting) or vaporization (boiling), the entropy of the reactant metal increases sharply, causing the overall reaction entropy change $\Delta S_{\text{rxn}}^\circ$ to become more negative and resulting in a sudden upward increase in the slope of the Ellingham line

C) The oxidation line for $2\text{C}(s) + \text{O}_2(g) \to 2\text{CO}(g)$ possesses a negative slope because one mole of gas produces two moles of gas ($\Delta n_g = +1$, so $\Delta S^\circ > 0$), meaning carbon monoxide becomes increasingly stable at elevated temperatures
D) The Ellingham diagram directly indicates the kinetic rate of the reduction reaction and allows the immediate calculation of the activation energy ($E_a$) for the reduction of any metal oxide
questions.explanation: Step 1: Applying the thermodynamic relation $\Delta G^\circ = \Delta H^\circ - T\Delta S^\circ$, differentiating with respect to temperature at constant pressure yields $\left(\frac{\partial \Delta G^\circ}{\partial T}\right)_P = -\Delta S^\circ$. Step 2: In reactions such as $2M(s) + \text{O}_2(g) \to 2MO(s)$, one mole of gas is converted to solid, so $\Delta S^\circ < 0$. Hence, the slope $-\Delta S^\circ$ is positive, confirming statement A. Step 3: When the reactant metal melts or vaporizes, its entropy increases ($S_{\text{metal}}$ rises). Since $\Delta S_{\text{rxn}}^\circ = S_{\text{oxide}} - (S_{\text{metal}} + S_{\text{O}_2})$, $\Delta S_{\text{rxn}}^\circ$ becomes significantly more negative. Consequently, the slope $-\Delta S_{\text{rxn}}^\circ$ increases abruptly upwards, confirming statement B. Step 4: For $2\text{C}(s) + \text{O}_2(g) \to 2\text{CO}(g)$, one mole of gaseous reactant produces two moles of gaseous product ($\Delta n_g = +1$), so $\Delta S^\circ > 0$. Therefore, $-\Delta S^\circ < 0$, giving a downward slope and increasing stability at higher temperatures, confirming statement C. Step 5: Statement D is incorrect because Ellingham diagrams are derived purely from equilibrium thermodynamics; they provide no information regarding reaction kinetics, mechanism, or activation energy.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: In the modern industrial Hall-Héroult electrometallurgical process for aluminium extraction, a molten solution of alumina ($\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$) in cryolite ($\text{Na}_3\text{AlF}_6$) and fluorspar ($\text{CaF}_2$) is electrolyzed at approximately $950^\circ\text{C}$ ($1223\text{ K}$) using carbon electrodes. Which of the following physicochemical statements regarding this process is/are correct?
options: A) The primary cathode reaction involves the direct six-electron reduction of complex fluoride anions to liberate elemental fluorine gas at the steel cathode shell

B) The carbon anode is sacrificially oxidized by electrochemically discharged oxy-anions, producing gaseous $\text{CO}_2$ and $\text{CO}$ via: $\text{C}(s) + 2\text{O}^{2-} \to \text{CO}_2(g) + 4e^-$ and $\text{C}(s) + \text{O}^{2-} \to \text{CO}(g) + 2e^-$, consuming approximately $0.5\text{ kg}$ of carbon per kilogram of aluminium produced

C) Addition of $\text{CaF}_2$ and $\text{AlF}_3$ depresses the bath melting point from $2050^\circ\text{C}$ to $\sim 950^\circ\text{C}$ and maintains the electrolyte density lower than that of liquid aluminium ($\rho_{\text{bath}} \approx 2.1\text{ g cm}^{-3} < \rho_{\text{Al}} \approx 2.3\text{ g cm}^{-3}$), allowing molten aluminium to settle at the cathode at the bottom

D) The undesirable 'anode effect' occurs when the local concentration of dissolved alumina drops below $\sim 1.0 - 1.5\%$, causing the bath to de-wet the anode and generating a resistive gas film of perfluorocarbons ($\text{CF}_4$ and $\text{C}_2\text{F}_6$), causing the cell voltage to surge from $\sim 4.5\text{ V}$ to over $30\text{ V}$
questions.explanation: Step 1: In the Hall-Héroult cell, cathode reduction deposits liquid aluminium via $\text{Al}^{3+} + 3e^- \to \text{Al}(l)$. Fluorine gas is never evolved at the cathode; statement A is false. Step 2: At the anode, oxygen-containing species (complex oxyfluoride ions $\text{Al}_2\text{OF}_6^{2-}$) discharge oxygen at carbon surfaces, reacting to form $\text{CO}_2$ and $\text{CO}$. Stoichiometrically, producing $1\text{ kg}$ of $\text{Al}$ requires $0.33 - 0.50\text{ kg}$ of carbon depending on the $\text{CO}_2/\text{CO}$ ratio, confirming statement B. Step 3: Pure alumina melts at $2050^\circ\text{C}$. The eutectic fluoride mixture ($sim 80\%\; \text{Na}_3\text{AlF}_6$, $5\%\; \text{CaF}_2$, $5\%\; \text{AlF}_3$, $10\%\; \text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$) melts below $950^\circ\text{C}$. Because molten aluminium is denser than the bath, it forms a protective liquid pool at the bottom, confirming statement C. Step 4: When dissolved alumina is depleted below $1.5\%$, fluoride ions discharge instead, forming insulating perfluorocarbon gases ($\text{CF}_4, \text{C}_2\text{F}_6$). This gas layer de-wets the graphite, creating an electric arc and causing a dramatic voltage surge known as the anode effect, confirming statement D.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: In the beneficiation of complex polymetallic sulfide ores (such as lead-zinc-copper ores) by froth flotation, mineral particles are selectively separated based on their interfacial wetting properties. Which of the following statements regarding the physical chemistry of froth flotation reagents is/are correct?
options: A) Collectors such as potassium ethyl xanthate ($\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OCS}_2\text{K}$) are amphiphilic heteropolar compounds whose polar thiocarbonate heads chemisorb onto the metal cations of sulfide minerals, orienting their hydrophobic hydrocarbon chains outward to increase the contact angle ($\theta > 90^\circ$)
B) Frothers such as pine oil and cresols act by increasing the surface tension of water, thereby causing rapid coalescence and collapse of air bubbles at the pulp surface

C) In the differential separation of $\text{PbS}$ from $\text{ZnS}$, sodium cyanide ($\text{NaCN}$) acts as a depressant for $\text{ZnS}$ by forming a hydrophilic, water-soluble coordination complex $[\text{Zn}(\text{CN})_4]^{2-}$ on the mineral surface, preventing collector adsorption

D) Subsequent flotation of depressed $\text{ZnS}$ is activated by adding copper(II) sulfate ($\text{CuSO}_4$), whereby $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ ions exchange with lattice $\text{Zn}^{2+}$ ions on the mineral surface ($\text{ZnS} + \text{Cu}^{2+} \to \text{CuS} + \text{Zn}^{2+}$), providing a copper sulfide surface layer that readily binds xanthate collectors
questions.explanation: Step 1: Froth flotation relies on differences in contact angle $\theta$. Collectors are surface-active surfactants with a polar ionic head and non-polar hydrocarbon tail. When the polar head chemisorbs onto mineral cations, the non-polar tail projects into the aqueous phase, rendering the mineral hydrophobic ($\theta > 90^\circ$) so it adheres to air bubbles, confirming statement A. Step 2: Frothers are amphiphilic molecules that adsorb at the gas-liquid interface, lowering the surface tension of water and preventing the coalescence of bubbles, thus stabilizing a persistent, fine froth; statement B is false because frothers lower surface tension, not raise it. Step 3: $\text{NaCN}$ acts as a depressant for $\text{ZnS}$ through chemical surface complexation, forming $[\text{Zn}(\text{CN})_4]^{2-}$, which prevents collector attachment and leaves $\text{ZnS}$ hydrophilic, confirming statement C. Step 4: Adding $\text{CuSO}_4$ activates $\text{ZnS}$ because the solubility product of $\text{CuS}$ ($K_{sp} \approx 10^{-36}$) is far smaller than that of $\text{ZnS}$ ($K_{sp} \approx 10^{-24}$). Copper ions replace zinc ions at the surface, forming a $\text{CuS}$ coating that readily chemisorbs xanthate, confirming statement D.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: Copper is extracted from chalcopyrite ($\text{CuFeS}_2$) through a multi-stage pyrometallurgical sequence involving roasting, smelting, Bessemerization, and electrolytic refining. Which of the following chemical statements regarding this sequence is/are correct?
options: A) During smelting in a reverberatory furnace, roasted ore melts to form two immiscible liquid layers: an upper molten silicate slag layer ($\text{FeSiO}_3$) and a dense lower layer known as copper matte (primarily $\text{Cu}_2\text{S}$ with minor $\text{FeS}$)

B) In the Bessemer converter, air is blown through molten matte in the presence of silica; iron sulfide is preferentially oxidized and slagged off first ($2\text{FeS} + 3\text{O}_2 \to 2\text{FeO} + 2\text{SO}_2$ and $\text{FeO} + \text{SiO}_2 \to \text{FeSiO}_3$) before copper sulfide undergoes self-reduction
C) Blister copper obtained directly from the Bessemer converter is $99.99\%$ pure and is directly drawn into wires without undergoing subsequent electrolytic refining

D) The self-reduction reaction $\text{Cu}_2\text{S} + 2\text{Cu}_2\text{O} \to 6\text{Cu}(l) + \text{SO}_2(g)$ yields crude copper whose solidified surface displays blisters due to the expulsion of dissolved $\text{SO}_2$ gas during freezing
questions.explanation: Step 1: In the smelting furnace, silica reacts with iron(II) oxide to form ferrous silicate slag: $\text{FeO} + \text{SiO}_2 \to \text{FeSiO}_3$. Slag has lower density and floats on top of the molten copper matte ($\text{Cu}_2\text{S} + \text{FeS}$), confirming statement A. Step 2: In the converter, iron has higher oxygen affinity than copper, so residual $\text{FeS}$ is oxidized first and removed as slag. After slag removal, copper sulfide undergoes partial oxidation to $\text{Cu}_2\text{O}$ and self-reduction: $\text{Cu}_2\text{S} + 2\text{Cu}_2\text{O} \to 6\text{Cu} + \text{SO}_2$, confirming statement B. Step 3: As molten copper solidifies, the solubility of sulfur dioxide drops drastically, and escaping $\text{SO}_2$ gas forms blisters on the surface of the cast metal, confirming statement D. Step 4: Statement C is false because blister copper is only about $98.0 - 99.0\%$ pure, containing impurities such as iron, nickel, zinc, silver, and gold. It has poor electrical conductivity and must undergo electrolytic refining to reach $99.99\%$ purity.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: Inside an iron blast furnace, solid charge (haematite, coke, limestone) descends while a reducing gas mixture ($\text{CO}, \text{CO}_2, \text{N}_2$) ascends under a steep temperature gradient ($500 - 2200\text{ K}$). Which of the following thermochemical statements regarding blast furnace operation is/are correct?
options: A) In the upper cooler stack ($500 - 900\text{ K}$), indirect reduction of iron oxides by $\text{CO}(g)$ ($3\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3 + \text{CO} \to 2\text{Fe}_3\text{O}_4 + \text{CO}_2$ and $\text{FeO} + \text{CO} \rightleftharpoons \text{Fe} + \text{CO}_2$) is thermodynamically preferred over direct reduction by carbon because $\Delta G^\circ$ for $\text{CO} \to \text{CO}_2$ is more negative than that for $\text{C} \to \text{CO}$

B) Direct reduction of wüstite by solid carbon ($\text{FeO} + \text{C} \to \text{Fe} + \text{CO}$) in the high-temperature zone is strongly exothermic and provides the primary thermal heat that melts the iron

C) The Boudouard equilibrium $\text{C}(s) + \text{CO}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{CO}(g)$ is endothermic ($\Delta H^\circ = +171\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$); hence, increasing temperature shifts the equilibrium toward $\text{CO}$, making $\text{CO}$ the dominant gas in the hotter reduction zones
D) Pig iron tapped from the hearth of the blast furnace has an extremely low carbon content of less than $0.1\%\; \text{C}$ by mass and exhibits high ductility
questions.explanation: Step 1: In the Ellingham diagram, the line for $2\text{CO} + \text{O}_2 \to 2\text{CO}_2$ lies below the $2\text{C} + \text{O}_2 \to 2\text{CO}$ line at temperatures below $983\text{ K}$. Hence, $\text{CO}$ is thermodynamically a more powerful reducing agent than carbon in the upper stack, confirming statement A. Step 2: The direct reduction reaction $\text{FeO} + \text{C} \to \text{Fe} + \text{CO}$ is endothermic ($\Delta H^\circ = +155\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$), requiring heat from coke combustion; statement B is false. Step 3: By Le Chatelier's principle, the endothermic Boudouard reaction $\text{C} + \text{CO}_2 \rightleftharpoons 2\text{CO}$ ($\Delta H^\circ > 0$) shifts strongly to the right above $1000\text{ K}$, regenerating $\text{CO}$ as the ascending gas moves through hotter coke, confirming statement C. Step 4: Statement D is false because pig iron tapped from the hearth contains about $4\%\; \text{C}$ along with impurities ($\text{Si}, \text{Mn}, \text{P}, \text{S}$), making it hard and brittle. Wrought iron (<0.2% C) is the purest and most ductile form.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText: Advanced refining techniques exploit specialized chemical equilibria and phase transitions to produce ultra-pure metals. Which of the following statements regarding these refining processes is/are correct?
options: A) Zone refining is capable of separating any impurity from a host metal, provided the equilibrium distribution coefficient $k = C_S/C_L$ is strictly equal to $1.00$

B) In Mond's process for refining nickel, the forward carbonylation $\text{Ni}(s) + 4\text{CO}(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{Ni}(\text{CO})_4(g)$ is exothermic ($\Delta H^\circ < 0$); hence, lower temperatures ($330 - 350\text{ K}$) favor formation of volatile carbonyl, while higher temperatures ($450 - 470\text{ K}$) shift the equilibrium toward endothermic thermal decomposition into pure nickel

C) In the Van Arkel-de Boer refining of titanium, the reaction vessel walls are maintained at $1800\text{ K}$ while the central tungsten wire is kept at $523\text{ K}$ to condense titanium tetraiodide

D) In zone refining of a semiconductor ingot, an impurity with an equilibrium partition coefficient $k < 1$ becomes progressively concentrated in the moving molten zone, resulting in solute enrichment at the trailing end of the bar after repeated passes
questions.explanation: Step 1: If $k = C_S/C_L = 1.00$, the impurity concentration in the solidifying solid is identical to that in the melt, meaning no segregation or purification can occur; statement A is false. Step 2: In Mond's process, $\text{Ni} + 4\text{CO} \rightleftharpoons \text{Ni}(\text{CO})_4$ is exothermic ($\Delta H^\circ = -160\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$). Lower temperatures ($330-350\text{ K}$) favor formation of the volatile tetracarbonyl, while higher temperatures ($450-470\text{ K}$) shift equilibrium to the left, decomposing it into pure metal and recycling $\text{CO}$, confirming statement B. Step 3: In the Van Arkel process, the vessel walls are kept at a lower temperature ($523\text{ K}$) to form $\text{TiI}_4(g)$, which decomposes on the electrically heated tungsten filament maintained at $1800\text{ K}$; statement C inverts the temperatures. Step 4: When $k < 1$, solute is rejected into the molten zone. Repeated unidirectional passes of the molten zone sweep the impurity forward, producing pure solid at the start and accumulating impurities at the trailing end, confirming statement D.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.questionText:
In the high-temperature zone of an iron blast furnace at $1000\text{ K}$, reduction of wüstite ($\text{FeO}$) by carbon monoxide and the Boudouard reaction are coupled according to the following equilibria:
$$(1) \quad \text{FeO}(s) + \text{CO}(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{Fe}(s) + \text{CO}_2(g), \quad \Delta G_1^\circ = -1.942\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$
$$(2) \quad \text{C}(s) + \text{CO}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{CO}(g), \quad \Delta G_2^\circ = -3.800\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$
Given $2.303 RT = 19.14\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ at $1000\text{ K}$ and assuming unit activities for all pure solid phases, determine the equilibrium partial pressure of carbon monoxide ($p_{\text{CO}}$) in bar for the net direct reduction: $\text{FeO}(s) + \text{C}(s) \rightleftharpoons \text{Fe}(s) + \text{CO}(g)$.
options: A) $2.0\text{ bar}$
B) $0.50\text{ bar}$
C) $4.0\text{ bar}$
D) $1.0\text{ bar}$
questions.explanation: Step 1: Adding reaction (1) and reaction (2) gives the net direct reduction reaction: $\text{FeO}(s) + \text{C}(s) \rightleftharpoons \text{Fe}(s) + \text{CO}(g)$. Step 2: The standard Gibbs free energy change for the net reaction is: $\Delta G_{\text{net}}^\circ = \Delta G_1^\circ + \Delta G_2^\circ = -1.942 + (-3.800) = -5.742\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$. Step 3: For this reaction, the equilibrium constant is $K_p = p_{\text{CO}}$ because all other participants are pure solids with unit activity. Step 4: Applying the thermodynamic relation: $\Delta G_{\text{net}}^\circ = -2.303 RT \log_{10} K_p$. Substituting the numerical values: $-5.742 = -19.14 \log_{10} p_{\text{CO}} \implies \log_{10} p_{\text{CO}} = \frac{5.742}{19.14} = 0.30$.
